subject: Anthropology
title: Caste Systems
description: A micro-lesson that makes Caste Systems usable.

hook.text: Born a Dalit, always a Dalit. India's caste system assigns your rank at birth. Mobility is almost forbidden.

buildup.text: Caste systems are rigid, hereditary social hierarchies where membership is determined by birth and reinforced by ritual.

discovery.text: India's system has four main varnas plus 'untouchables.' Purity rules govern contact, food, and marriage between castes.

twist.text: Caste-like systems exist beyond India. Japan's burakumin and Rwanda's Tutsi-Hutu division show that caste is not unique.

climax.text: Caste reveals how inequality can be made sacred. When hierarchy is divine law, challenging it becomes unthinkable.

punchline.text: The cruelest inequality is the kind you cannot question.

quiz.question: What defines a caste system?
options: Rigid, hereditary hierarchy determined by birth and reinforced by ritual

details.summary: Caste systems are hierarchical social classifications inherited at birth that determine marriage partners, occupation, and social status. India's caste system is the most studied, but caste-like stratification exists in many other societies worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Caste demonstrates how kinship and social hierarchy interlock to create enduring inequality. Understanding caste helps explain how birth-based stratification persists even when formally abolished by law.
takeaways: Caste is a birth-based hierarchical system governing marriage and status
India's system is best known but caste-like structures exist globally
Caste persists socially even when legally abolished

faq.question: How does caste differ from social class?
faq.answer: Class is theoretically mobile — you can move up or down through achievement. Caste is ascribed at birth and cannot be changed through individual effort. Caste boundaries are maintained through endogamy, ritual purity rules, and occupational restrictions.

faq.question: Does caste discrimination still exist in modern India?
faq.answer: Yes, despite being constitutionally banned since 1950. Caste continues to affect marriage choices, employment opportunities, social interactions, and political mobilization. Urban environments and education reduce but do not eliminate caste-based discrimination.
